questions.text: Consider a relational table R that is in 3NF, but not in BCNF. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.solution:
3NF allows [latex]X\rightarrow A[/latex] with X not a superkey only when A is a prime attribute. BCNF forbids it.

So a relation in 3NF but not in BCNF must have such an FD with prime A. The other options describe 3NF/2NF violations or a 1NF violation.

Answer: X [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] A where X is not a superkey and A is a prime attribute

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: R has a nontrivial functional dependency [latex]X\rightarrow A[/latex], where X is not a superkey and A is a prime attribute.
R has a nontrivial functional dependency [latex]X\rightarrow A[/latex], where X is not a superkey and A is a non-prime attribute and X is not a proper subset of any key.
R has a nontrivial functional dependency [latex]X\rightarrow A[/latex], where X is not a superkey and A is a non-prime attribute and X is a proper subset of some key.
A cell in R holds a set instead of an atomic value.

Conflicting pairs in the given schedule (their order must be kept):

questions.text:
An organization requires a range of IP address to assign one to each of its 1500 computers. The organization has approached an Internet Service Provider (ISP) for this task. The ISP uses CIDR and serves the requests from the available IP address space 202.61.0.0/17. The ISP wants to assign an address space to the organization which will minimize the number of routing entries in the ISP?s router using route aggregation. Which of the following address spaces are potential candidates from which the ISP can allot any one of the organization?

I. 202.61.84.0/21
II. 202.61.104.0/21
III. 202.61.64.0/21
IV. 202.61.144.0/21
questions.solution:
1500 hosts need [latex]2^{11}=2048[/latex] addresses [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] a /21 block. A /21 must start at a third octet that is a multiple of 8, and lie inside 202.61.0.0/17 (third octet 0-127).

- I: 84 is not a multiple of 8 False
- II: 104 = 13 [latex]\times[/latex] 8 True
- III: 64 = 8 [latex]\times[/latex] 8 True
- IV: 144 is outside the /17 range False

Answer: II and III only

questions.text:
Which one of the following predicate formulae is NOT logically valid?
Note that W is a predicate formula without any free occurrence of x.
questions.solution:
Since x is not free in W:
- [latex]\forall x(p(x)\vee W)\equiv\forall x\,p(x)\vee W[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] valid.
- [latex]\exists x(p(x)\wedge W)\equiv\exists x\,p(x)\wedge W[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] valid.
- [latex]\forall x(p(x)\rightarrow W)\equiv\forall x(\neg p(x)\vee W)\equiv\neg\exists x\,p(x)\vee W\equiv\exists x\,p(x)\rightarrow W[/latex], not [latex]\forall x\,p(x)\rightarrow W[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] not valid.
- [latex]\exists x(p(x)\rightarrow W)\equiv\neg\forall x\,p(x)\vee W\equiv\forall x\,p(x)\rightarrow W[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] valid.

Answer: Option 3

questions.text:
Let [latex]G=(V,E)[/latex] be a directed, weighed graph with weight function [latex]w:E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}[/latex]. For some function [latex]f:V\rightarrow \mathbb{R}[/latex], for each edge [latex](u,v) \in E[/latex], define [latex]w'(u,v)[/latex] as [latex]w(u,v)+f(u)-f(v)[/latex].

Which one of the options completes the following sentence so that it is TRUE?

"The shortest paths in G under [latex]w[/latex] are shortest paths under [latex]w'[/latex] too,_________".
questions.solution:
For any path [latex]s=v_0\rightarrow v_1\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow v_k=t[/latex], the f-terms cancel in pairs:
[latex]w'(\text{path})=w(\text{path})+f(s)-f(t)[/latex]

Every s-to-t path changes by the same constant [latex]f(s)-f(t)[/latex], so the shortest one stays shortest, for any f. (This is the reweighting trick in Johnson's algorithm.)

Answer: for every [latex]f:V\rightarrow\mathbb{R}[/latex]

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: if and only if [latex]\forall u \in V,f(u)[/latex] is positive
if and only if [latex]\forall u \in V,f(u)[/latex] is negative
if and only if f(u) is the distance from s to u in the graph obtained by adding a new vertex s to G and edges of zero weight from s to every verex of G
